title: EigenBench: A Comparative Behavioral Measure of Value Alignment
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: A multi-stage procedure turns pairwise judgments from an ensemble of models into a single consensus ranking of alignment.
layout: 5 numbered step panels, left-to-right with snaking arrows, worked example text inside boxes
description: A five-step flowchart on a light gray background, with each stage in a gray panel under a dark gray header. Step 1 (left) shows the inputs: a blue box for the set of scenarios, a green box with a quoted constitution, and a list of colored model bars with logos (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek). Step 2 (bottom left) shows a sample scenario about human extinction. Step 3 (center) shows a judge box (orange-red) quoting its verdict. Two evaluee response boxes (blue for DeepSeek, dark gray for Grok) sit below it, and a peach box of pairwise comparison data sits above. Step 4 (top right) shows Bradley-Terry-Davidson fitting, with a loss formula and learned parameters. Step 5 (bottom right) shows the trust-matrix formula, a Perron-Frobenius eigenvector update, and final Elo ratings. Black arrows connect the boxes. The eye lands first on the large colored judge and evaluee text boxes in the center.
caption: The EigenBench Pipeline: Starting with a population of models M = {M1, . . . , MN}, a constitution C, and a set of prompted scenarios S, we repeatedly sample a scenario Sℓ∈S, prompt a pair of models Mj, Mk with the scenario, prompt a third model Mi to judge which response is more aligned to C, fit the resulting judgments rijkl to a Bradley-Terry-Davidson model of pairwise preferences to learn model dispositions and judge lenses in a latent space Rd, derive a trust matrix indicating how often judge Mi favors evaluee Mj’s responses, extract the left eigenvector t of the trust matrix, and convert t to Elo ratings that indicate, in the aggregate judgment of the population M, each model’s degree of alignment to C. Importantly, only the judge receives the constitution; the evaluees do not know what criteria will be used to evaluate their responses (or even that they will be evaluated at all).
abstract: Aligning AI with human values is a pressing unsolved problem. To address the lack of quantitative metrics for value alignment, we propose EigenBench: a black-box method for comparatively benchmarking language models' values. Given an ensemble of models, a constitution describing a value system, and a dataset of scenarios, our method returns a vector of scores quantifying each model's alignment to the given constitution. To produce these scores, each model judges the outputs of other models across many scenarios, and these judgments are aggregated with EigenTrust (Kamvar et al., 2003), yielding scores that reflect a weighted consensus judgment of the whole ensemble. EigenBench uses no ground truth labels, as it is designed to quantify subjective traits for which reasonable judges may disagree on the correct label. Hence, to validate our method, we collect human judgments on the same ensemble of models and show that EigenBench's judgments align closely with those of human evaluators. We further demonstrate that EigenBench can recover model rankings on the GPQA benchmark without access to objective labels, supporting its viability as a framework for evaluating subjective values for which no ground truths exist. The code is available at https://github.com/jchang153/EigenBench.
